content.content:
Each step runs in the lane of the work it does, as the [PromptSendingScope](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says: the Chain task and its spec follow-up in the spec lane, the code step in the code lane. A step is sent once the step before it finishes, never before, and goes to the head of its lane's queue, ahead of the prompts already waiting there, so it runs as soon as that lane is free, and straight away if it already is. The lane it leaves is free for its own queue meanwhile, so a Spec task sent while a chain's code step runs runs beside it. A step waiting for its lane shows in the queue like any prompt, and can be cancelled there, ending the chain. A step whose chain step before it failed or was cancelled is never sent.
In the previous tasks list, a chain's steps are grouped under one parent item, so they read as parts of a single chain. The parent is a heading row in the list, tinted the Chain colour, as the [PromptModesScope](./modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) colours it, a little more strongly than a single task's tint: a joined chain icon, the first line of the prompt, and at its right how many steps it has, "2 steps" or "3 steps". Its status is the chain's as a whole: Running while any step runs, Failed or Cancelled if a step was, and otherwise that of its last step. It has no checkbox, Resend, or Send to the other mode of its own, and clicking it doesn't open anything.
Beneath it, each step stays an item of its own, exactly as any previous task is, with its checkbox, status, Resend, and whatever else a task offers, opening onto its own prompt, table, and changed files. The steps are indented from the parent, joined to it by a thin line in the Chain colour down their left, from the parent's heading to the last step, and each is labelled by what it did, "Spec", "Code", or "Spec follow-up", in that step's mode colour, before its prompt, which leaves out the prompt's first line when it is the parent's. They are listed in the order they ran.
A chain is listed where its first step was sent, oldest first like every other item; tasks sent while it ran, such as questions or tasks of the other lane run between its steps, are never listed within it, and are listed after the chain, in the order they were sent. A chain's steps are found by which step each was sent from, not by being next to each other in the history. A chain still running, or one whose later steps haven't been sent yet, shows as many steps as have been, and a step still running shows as it would anywhere. When the latest task, heading the view, is a step of a chain, that chain's earlier steps are still grouped under its parent in the list, the parent saying the rest is the latest task. A session divider never falls between a chain's steps: it goes above the chain's parent. A step from the history whose chain can't be worked out, as when the step it was sent from is missing, is listed as a task of its own.

#### Header

The latest task heads the view whether or not the harness is working. It is the task sent most recently, whichever lane it runs in; a task still running in the other lane is among the previous tasks, shown running there, as any previous task is. The header shows its status, with a spinner while it is under way, the name of the hidden anchor it was compiled from, and the compiled markdown the harness actually received, which scrolls once it gets tall. Until it has compiled, the prompt as typed is shown instead. At its right, a Resend button sends it again, as the [PromptSendingScope](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says. The header shows the prompt the task was sent with, however much is sent to it while it runs; what is sent is shown in its output.
However long the compiled prompt, a prompt sent with its spec slices included, the header lays out only what is in view: the prompt is split into its blocks of markdown, paragraphs, headings, lists, and code blocks, each drawn as it scrolls into view, as the rows of a table are, so a long prompt costs no more to show, scroll, or animate than a short one. The header is as tall as the prompt up to where it starts to scroll.

#### Header

The latest task heads the view whether or not the harness is working. It is always the most recent task still active: of the tasks under way, building, compiling, or running, in either lane, the one sent most recently. Only while no task is under way is it the task that finished most recently, or, before any has finished, the one sent most recently. A finished task never heads the view while another is under way: when it finishes while a task in the other lane still runs, that task heads the view in its place at once, and the task that finished goes among the previous tasks. So with two Chain tasks sent one after the other, once both their spec steps have finished, the first chain's code step heads the view while it runs, not the second chain's finished spec step, and the second chain's code step heads it in turn once it is sent. A task still running in the other lane that is not the latest is among the previous tasks, shown running there, as any previous task is. Whichever task heads the view, its header and output show as they do for a task just sent, and the previous tasks, their row's count, and the chain grouping follow it. The header shows its status, with a spinner while it is under way, the name of the hidden anchor it was compiled from, and the compiled markdown the harness actually received, which scrolls once it gets tall. Until it has compiled, the prompt as typed is shown instead. At its right, a Resend button sends it again, as the [PromptSendingScope](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says. The header shows the prompt the task was sent with, however much is sent to it while it runs; what is sent is shown in its output.
However long the compiled prompt, a prompt sent with its spec slices included, the header lays out only what is in view: the prompt is split into its blocks of markdown, paragraphs, headings, lists, and code blocks, each drawn as it scrolls into view, as the rows of a table are, so a long prompt costs no more to show, scroll, or animate than a short one. The header is as tall as the prompt up to where it starts to scroll.

content.text:
I've changed the spec so the task heading the message list is always the most recent task still running. The code isn't changed yet. `piton check` found no problems and `piton build` wrote 75 files.

**What changed in the spec**

All of it is in the Header part of the prompt editor (`spec/scope/prompt-mode/index.pi`). Before, the task heading the view was simply the one sent most recently, even if it had already finished. Now:

- **Which task heads the view:** of the tasks still under way (building, compiling or running) in either lane, the one sent most recently.
- **When nothing is under way:** the task that finished most recently, or before any has finished, the one sent most recently.
- **A finished task never stays on top while another is running:** when it finishes and the other lane still has a task running, that running task takes over the view at once. The finished task moves into the previous tasks.
- **Your example is written into the spec:** two Chain tasks are sent, and both spec steps finish. The first chain's code step heads the view while it runs, not the second chain's finished spec step. The second chain's code step heads the view once it is sent.
- **Everything else follows the task on top:** its header and output show as for a newly sent task. The previous tasks list, its count and the chain grouping all treat the task on top as the latest. "Send to task" already goes to whichever task that is.

**Anchors the code should follow**
- `.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/index.md#header` is the new rule.
- Unchanged but relevant:
  - `#chained-tasks` and `#previous-tasks` in the same file.
  - `.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/sending/index.md#lanes`.
  - The "Send to task" and Cancel text in `.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope`.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1790931264-DisplayMostRecentActiveTask.understanding.md`.
